name: ode
why: The Open Dynamics Engine simulates articulated rigid body physics, a real simulation you can drive and disturb.

brief.what_it_is: ODE (Open Dynamics Engine) is an open-source C/C++ library for simulating articulated rigid body dynamics. You give it bodies, joints, and forces through its API, and each simulation step it advances the physics state. It has built-in collision detection with friction, and it can use OPCODE or GIMPACT for triangle-mesh collisions. The README describes it as a library rather than a standalone program, so the Homebrew executable ode-config is presumably a build-flag helper for projects that link against it; the README does not mention ode-config. The homepage and README describe uses in ground vehicles, legged creatures, and VR objects.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames ODE as a physics SDK: a library that a game or simulation program embeds to get rigid-body motion and contact handling without writing its own solver. The homepage says it is "currently used in many computer games, 3D authoring tools and simulation tools."
brief.how_it_works: The README does not explain the solver internals. It says ODE has advanced joint types, integrated collision detection with friction, and a C/C++ API. Its build options include ODE_DOUBLE_PRECISION for double-precision math and ODE_WITH_OPCODE for trimesh collisions, which are the main knobs a user would touch.

brief.install_notes: Requires CMake 3.10 or later and a C/C++ compiler (GCC, Clang, MSVC, or MinGW). OpenGL and GLU are needed only for the demos, which are on by default (ODE_WITH_DEMOS=ON); turn them off with -DODE_WITH_DEMOS=OFF if you only want the library. The README gives per-platform steps for Windows (Visual Studio, MSYS2), Linux, and macOS, and lists Xcode and Visual Studio generators. No accounts, runtimes, or first-run configuration are mentioned. The README's install steps are for building from source; it does not mention a Homebrew formula or a separate ode-config step.
brief.standout: It is a physics engine you drive from code and then perturb, so the fun is in changing forces, joints, or collisions and watching the simulated bodies respond. Its demos are built with an OpenGL-based DrawStuff library, which makes it a visual playground rather than only a library.
brief.status: maintained. The GitHub repository at github.com/odedevs/ode has CI badges for Windows, MSYS2, Ubuntu, Arch Linux, and macOS, and its copyright line runs through 2026 ("Copyright (C) 2008-2026 Open Dynamics Engine contributors"). I did not see a release date or last-commit date. The ode.org homepage is old-looking, with a 2001-2004 copyright and mailing-list archives from 2007, and it still points to BitBucket, which I could not read.
brief.caveats: The homepage is dated and still points to BitBucket for source; the live repository is on GitHub. Triangle-mesh collisions via GIMPACT are marked experimental. The LGPL and BSD licenses both apply, and the README notes third-party code (GIMPACT, libccd, OU/ODER, OPCODE) under its own licenses. The README does not mention ode-config, so I could not confirm what the Homebrew executable does. The BitBucket README fetch returned only page chrome.
quotes: ODE is a free, industrial quality library for simulating articulated rigid body dynamics - for example ground vehicles, legged creatures, and moving objects in VR environments.
It is fast, flexible, robust and platform independent, with advanced joints, contact with friction, and built-in collision detection.
It is fully featured, stable, mature and platform independent with an easy to use C/C++ API.
